articleBody:
Creating a comfortable secondary living suite for an aging parent requires balancing personal autonomy with safety and accessibility. A thoughtful layout avoids common mobility hazards while blending seamlessly into the home.

- [ ] Zero-threshold exterior and interior entryways — eliminating raised doorway sills prevents tripping hazards for walkers and wheelchairs.
- [ ] Minimum 36-inch wide interior doorways — wide passage frames allow easy movement between rooms without scraping knuckles or bumping equipment.
- [ ] Reinforced bathroom wall blocking — hidden wooden backing behind drywall allows secure installation of grab bars near toilets and showers either now or later.
- [ ] Curbless walk-in shower with bench seating — a roll-in, lip-free shower pan eliminates the dangerous step over a tub edge.
- [ ] Lever-style handles on all doors and plumbing fixtures — levers are much easier to turn for hands dealing with arthritis compared to round knobs.
- [ ] Slip-resistant tile flooring with tight grout lines — smooth, matte surfaces reduce slip potential while supporting steady foot traction.
- [ ] Raised electrical outlets and rocker light switches — placing outlets slightly higher reduces deep bending, while large rockers are simple to tap.
- [ ] Dedicated mini-split temperature controls — personal climate management keeps the suite comfortable without forcing household-wide thermostat battles.
- [ ] Accessible galley kitchenette with low-profile counters — lower prep areas and shallow sinks make light meal prep safe and independent.

How to use this checklist:
Walk through your proposed living space with this list in hand before framing or rough plumbing begins. Verifying structural blocking, doorway openings, and plumbing rough-ins during early construction avoids costly tear-outs after the drywall is finished.
